title: How Greggs Got So Profitable Selling Sausage Rolls

beats.say: A bakery that started with one man delivering eggs and yeast on a bicycle now sells more than two billion pounds of food a year. And a lot of it is sausage rolls.

vis.text: From a bicycle to £2 billion a year.

beats.say: Greggs is on almost every high street in Britain. In twenty twenty five it sold two point one five billion pounds of food, and opened more than two hundred new shops in a single year.
So how did a Newcastle bakery become one of the biggest food chains in the country, while selling things for a couple of quid? Let's find out.

vis.text: How do you get rich selling £1 sausage rolls?

beats.say: Part one. The bicycle.
Greggs started in Newcastle in nineteen thirty nine, when John Gregg delivered eggs and yeast to local people by bike. His first shop came later, in Gosforth.

events: John Gregg starts a delivery round in Newcastle
The first Greggs shop opens in Gosforth

beats.say: For decades it was a regional bakery. But the business learned one lesson early, and it's the secret to everything that came after: make it yourself.

vis.text: Greggs makes its own food in its own factories
vis.date: Then sends it to thousands of shops

beats.say: Part two. Make it yourself.
Most of what you buy in a Greggs isn't baked from scratch in the back of the shop. It's made in Greggs' own manufacturing sites, then delivered to the shops and finished in the ovens.
When you own the factory, the lorries and the shops, nobody else in the middle takes a cut. That's called vertical integration, and it lets Greggs keep prices low while still making money.
It also means every shop sells almost exactly the same thing. Fewer recipes, made in huge numbers, the same way every time. That's how you make a sausage roll cheaply, millions of times over.
Greggs even sells its food in other people's shops. You can find Greggs sausage rolls and bakes in the freezer at Iceland supermarkets, so people can eat Greggs at home without ever going into one.
Part three. Volume, not margin.

Greggs doesn't make a fortune on each item. In twenty twenty five, its underlying profit before tax was about one hundred and seventy two million pounds, on two point one five billion in sales. That's roughly eight pence profit for every pound you spend.

vis.label: profit from every £1 spent (roughly)
vis.source: Greggs 2025: underlying profit before tax £171.9m on sales of £2.151bn

beats.say: Eight pence isn't much. But multiply it by millions of customers, every single day, in thousands of shops, and it adds up to a lot of money.

And that's why Greggs is obsessed with opening more shops. In twenty twenty five it opened two hundred and seven new ones and closed thirty six, ending the year with two thousand seven hundred and thirty nine.

vis.title: Greggs shops in 2025
vis.source: Greggs 2025 trading update: 2,739 shops at year end

beats.say: It says there's room for significantly more than three thousand shops in the UK. Train stations. Motorway services. Drive-thrus. Supermarkets. Anywhere people are hungry and in a hurry.
Every new shop is another place to sell the same cheap food from the same factories. The factories and lorries are already paid for, so each extra shop makes the whole machine more efficient.

vis.text: Same factories. More shops. More profit per lorry.

beats.say: Greggs also pushes deals that get you to spend a little more. A breakfast deal with a coffee. A meal deal at lunch. An app that rewards you for coming back. Each one nudges the average spend up by a few pence, and a few pence times millions is a lot.
Part four. The vegan sausage roll moment.
In January twenty nineteen, Greggs launched a vegan sausage roll. Some people were furious. A famous TV presenter complained about it online. And Greggs replied with a joke.

vis.text: Greggs launches a vegan sausage roll, and the internet goes wild

beats.say: The row was the best advertising Greggs never paid for. Suddenly everyone was talking about a bakery chain, and people queued up to try it. Greggs stopped being just a cheap lunch, and became something people talked about.

vis.title: How a row became a win

beats.say: Since then, Greggs has leaned into the joke. Clothing collaborations. A Greggs pop-up that looked like a fancy restaurant. It's turned a sausage roll into a brand.

vis.text: It turned a sausage roll into a brand.

beats.say: Part five. Opening later.

Greggs used to be a breakfast and lunch shop. Now nearly three quarters of its shops stay open after five in the evening, and evenings are its fastest growing time of day. Add delivery apps, and the same shop can sell more without needing more space.

In the evening, the menu changes too. Hot food like pizza and wedges is aimed at people heading home from work or out for the night. It's the same shop and the same staff, selling to a completely new crowd.

So what's the catch? Costs. Wages, energy and ingredients have all gone up, and in twenty twenty five Greggs' profit actually fell, even though sales rose. Building new distribution centres was expensive too.
And when the whole business depends on being cheap, it's hard to raise prices without customers noticing. That's the tightrope Greggs walks every day.

vis.text: Cheap is the brand. Costs keep rising.

beats.say: But the formula is simple. Make it yourself. Keep the menu small. Sell millions of them. And open a shop wherever people are hungry.
Not bad for a business that started with a bicycle and a basket of eggs.

vis.text: Not bad for a bicycle and some eggs.

beats.say: Subscribe for more on how businesses really make their money. And tell me in the comments, which Greggs item is the best?
